newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Trans-World eyes Norilsk stake but on new terms.
newsitem.headline: Trans-World eyes Norilsk stake but on new terms.

text.p: Trans-World Group, the UK-based commodities powerhouse, wants to bid for 38 percent of Russia's mining giant Norilsk Nickel but only if the terms of the tender are changed, legal and company sources said Friday.

Russian commercial bank Uneximbank announced earlier this month it would offer its 38 percent Norilsk stake in an investment tender opening July 22. It is still unclear whether the tender is open to foreign bidders or not.

"Subject to the terms of the tender being consistent with international standards, Trans-World would take part in the tender," said Eric Bettelheim of lawyers Mayer, Brown and Platt, representing the commodity group.
A Trans-World letter cited in a company news release asked the Russian government to cancel the planned auction to allow for a new tender based on what it called accepted international terms.
In the letter, addressed to President Boris Yeltsin and other senior officials, the group said the tender's current terms were "the biggest mistake in the history of Russian industry".
It added, "The State of Russia is about to lose one of its most attractive industrial enterprises...because of the disadvantageous terms of the auction."

Trans-World said the tender was being held too quickly and potential buyers were being asked to bid on a multi-billion dollar asset without receiving a full international audit or review of the state of the group's flagship metals plant.

Uneximbank received control of the 38 percent stake, which represents 51 percent of voting shares in the Norilsk group, in a government share-for-loans scheme in 1995. The bank has announced it intends to bid in the tender.
Trans-World said the fact a bidder was also the owner of the stake and so close to the organisation of the auction raised questions over competition among bidders.
"Without qualified competitive bids, one of Russia's industrial treasures will be sold off at bargain basement prices," David Reuben, Trans-World chairman, said in the statement.

Trans-World said it was willing to provide loan funds at the LIBOR rate to reimburse current owners for return of the shares to the state pending the tender, and would lend another $10 million in funds to pay for full supervision of the sale.

It also recommended the current tender be cancelled and that international and Russian investors should bid one year before the sale was carried out. Under the current timetable the results of the sale will be announced on August 5.

Norilsk is vying to become the world's biggest nickel producer in 1997 with over 20 percent of the world market. It is also the world's largest producer of palladium and a major producer of platinum, copper and cobalt.
But huge social costs and regional and federal debts have undermined its financial position.
Analysts said Western nickel producers such as Canada's Falconbridge and Inco, as well as major commodity companies, could be interested in bidding for the stake if they were allowed.
The starting price for the stake is around $117 million, and the winner would also have to invest $300 million in the group and cancel debts worth $70 million.
Trans-World is already a major player in Russia's huge aluminium industry and is said to control a major stake in Russia's Novolipetsk steel plant.
